question: Article 349 of the Treaty on European Union sets out the scope of application for the outermost territories, which include the Canary Islands owing to their structural social and economic situation. However, according to the Spanish Constitution the Canaries are an archipelago.

Under Article 46(b) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) – ratified by Spain on 14 February 1997 – an archipelago means ‘a group of islands, including parts of islands, interconnecting waters and other natural features which are so closely interrelated that such islands, waters and other natural features form an intrinsic geographical, economic and political entity, or which historically have been regarded as such’.
How does the Commission intend to bring the definition of the Canary Islands into line in European legislation and replace it with Canaries archipelago?
Does the Commission see any possibility of revising the Treaty on European Union in this respect?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.6.2024) With the term ‘Canary Islands’, Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) refers to that outermost region as defined in the Spanish legal order. As the text of this provision leaves no room for ambiguity as regards the territory to which it applies, the Commission considers that no revision of the Treaty is necessary.

Article 349 TFEU recognises the permanent constraints of the outermost regions1 (including the Canary Islands), such as remoteness, insularity, small size, difficult topography and climate, and economic dependence on a small number of sectors.

The Treaty therefore provides for specific measures to support these regions, including the adapted application of EU law and access to EU programmes, as reflected in the 2022 Communication on the EU’s outermost regions2.
